exam: What is the most specific test to confirm hereditary elliptocytosis? — Peripheral blood smear showing >10% elliptocytes; negative Coombs test.
A 6‑year‑old presents with pallor and splenomegaly; smear shows elliptocytes. What is the next best step? — Assess haemoglobin; if <7 g/dL, transfuse; otherwise monitor.
Why is splenectomy avoided in most cases of hereditary elliptocytosis? — It removes the site of haemolysis but increases infection risk; reserved for refractory cases.
How would you differentiate hereditary elliptocytosis from malaria‑induced haemolysis? — Look for parasites on smear; malaria shows trophozoites, not elliptocytes; Coombs negative.
What complication is most likely if a patient with hereditary elliptocytosis develops severe anaemia? — Hypersplenism leading to pancytopenia.
In a low‑resource setting, which investigation is essential if the patient cannot afford a Coombs test? — A simple peripheral smear and reticulocyte count to assess haemolysis.
What is the main reason to counsel families about genetic testing? — To inform future pregnancy planning and identify at‑risk siblings.
ai.title: Hereditary Elliptocytosis
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A red‑cell membrane defect causing elliptocytes on smear, leading to mild to severe haemolytic anaemia. Diagnosis relies on morphology and family history, with limited tests in low‑resource settings.

b: Family history of anaemia or splenomegaly
sections.p: Hereditary elliptocytosis is a congenital red‑cell membrane defect characterised by elliptically shaped erythrocytes on peripheral smear. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and may coexist with other membrane disorders.

b: Severe: significant pallor, splenomegaly, transfusion need
sections.p: Severity is graded by haemoglobin level and clinical impact: mild (Hb 10–12 g/dL), moderate (Hb 7–10 g/dL), severe (Hb <7 g/dL) or symptomatic anaemia. Splenomegaly and transfusion requirement further stratify risk.

The primary cause is mutations in spectrin, protein 4.1, or band 3 genes affecting membrane skeleton integrity. Secondary causes include nutritional deficiencies and infections common in the tropics that exacerbate haemolysis.
Children may present with pallor, fatigue, jaundice, or splenomegaly. In low‑resource settings, anaemia is often misattributed to malaria or nutritional deficiencies.
Investigation priorities focus on confirming haemolysis and excluding other causes. In settings lacking advanced tests, a simple smear and basic biochemistry suffice.
Urgent care is needed for severe anaemia, haemodynamic instability, or massive splenomegaly. Complications include hypersplenism, iron overload, and gallstones.

b: Transfusion for Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic anaemia
sections.p: Management is supportive: treat anaemia, avoid splenectomy unless refractory, and counsel on avoiding triggers. In low‑resource settings, focus on transfusion and monitoring.
